analysis.one_liner: Directs COVID-19 relief funds to nursing home protective gear, testing, and outbreak response teams while renewing elder-abuse prevention programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of the four House committees it was sent to, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required a share of future coronavirus relief money to buy protective equipment and testing for nursing home staff and residents, and to fund rapid-response medical teams for outbreak facilities. It would have forced nursing homes to report COVID-19 cases and deaths daily, made that data public, and reauthorized federal grants that fund long-term care ombudsmen, adult protective services, and elder abuse investigations. It also proposed stronger tracking of nursing home quality ratings, guardianship oversight, and automatic revocation of drug registrations for providers kicked out of Medicare for improper opioid prescribing.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and assisted living residents, who were dying at extreme rates during the pandemic, would get protective equipment, free regular testing, and strike teams sent to facilities with outbreaks. Staff at those facilities get the same protections. Elderly and disabled adults facing abuse or neglect would benefit from continued ombudsman grants, expanded adult protective services funding, and new ways of detecting abuse through Medicare and Medicaid claims data. Families would gain daily public reporting of cases and deaths at each facility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents, staff, and abuse victims

how_it_helps.text: A portion of COVID-19 relief appropriations would be reserved for protective equipment and free regular testing for nursing home staff and residents, including assisted living facilities [S2][S3].

States would establish strike teams — assessment, testing, and clinical crews — to respond to COVID-19 outbreaks in nursing facilities, and must alert state regulators and Medicaid fraud units within 18 hours if a team finds care problems that immediately endanger residents [S3].

Nursing homes and long-term care facilities would have to report all suspected and confirmed COVID-19 cases and all deaths going back to January 1, 2020, on a daily basis, and the government would publish that data publicly [S2][S3].

The bill reauthorizes through FY2023 grants for state long-term care ombudsman programs ($12 million a year), elder abuse forensic centers ($10 million a year), and adult protective services, plus a one-time $60 million in direct payments to state and tribal adult protective services agencies during the emergency [S2][S3].
Medicare and Medicaid claims data would be used to flag potential physical or sexual abuse or neglect of residents, and direct-care staff would be required to get training on the signs of abuse [S3].

If the Health and Human Services Secretary revokes a provider's Medicare enrollment for improper prescribing of controlled substances, the Attorney General would be required to revoke that provider's DEA drug registration [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost is carried by federal coronavirus relief accounts, which would be partially redirected from their original purposes, and by a one-time $20 million transfer from the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund. Nursing homes would bear the administrative burden of daily case and death reporting and payroll-based staffing data submissions.
analysis.who_pays_short: COVID relief funds and the Medicare trust fund

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify how much relief money would be diverted, only that 'a portion' of any future COVID-19 appropriations be used for PPE, testing, and strike teams, leaving the actual scale of support undefined [S3].

Many of its provisions are studies, guidance documents, reports, and a task force — such as a review of the Five-Star nursing home rating system and a racial disparities task force — that would produce recommendations rather than immediate changes in care [S3].

Daily public reporting of every case and death, plus resumed payroll-based staffing data submission, adds real administrative cost to facilities already struggling with staffing during the pandemic, and the bill offsets its own work with a $20 million transfer out of the Medicare Hospital Insurance Trust Fund [S3].

Opponents of transparency mandates would argue that publicizing facility-level death counts during a pandemic could expose facilities to liability and public backlash without additional funding attached to the reporting requirement itself [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions — guaranteed PPE, free testing, outbreak strike teams, and public daily death reporting — address what was by far the deadliest setting in the American COVID-19 outbreak, and the price is a modest redirection of relief money already being spent. The weaknesses are that the funding share is unspecified and several sections are studies and reports that would have delivered little during the emergency itself. On balance a well-designed, targeted bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late August 2020 and referred to four House committees, none of which ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ann Wagner introduced the bill on August 25, 2020, with Mr. Hill of Arkansas as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].

The same day, it was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — a multi-committee referral that requires each panel to act on the provisions in its jurisdiction before a bill can advance [S1][S5].
No committee held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it out, and no floor vote ever occurred [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and all bills not passed by then die automatically [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators are better off: they avoided mandatory daily public reporting of COVID-19 cases and deaths, disclosure of payroll-based staffing data, enhanced federal oversight of the worst-performing facilities, and a reweighting of the star rating system. The proposed $60 million for adult protective services and renewed ombudsman and elder abuse grants also never happened, so state elder-protection programs did not receive the new money.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators, who avoided new reporting and oversight

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but since the bill never reached a vote, no one's actual position was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: The bill would have sent the industry dedicated PPE, free testing, outbreak strike teams, and flexible use of emergency funds, while imposing daily public reporting of cases and deaths, payroll staffing disclosures, and stronger federal oversight. Its interest in the funding ran alongside residents' interests; its interest in avoiding the transparency and oversight mandates ran against them.

industries.industry: Assisted living and residential care facilities
industries.note: These facilities, which are not Medicare-participating providers, would have been covered by the PPE, testing, reporting, and televisit requirements for the first time in this bill, receiving support while taking on reporting duties.

industries.industry: Pharmacies and prescribers of controlled substances
industries.note: Providers stripped of Medicare enrollment for improper prescribing would automatically lose DEA registration, tightening enforcement against overprescribing.
